Bulleh Shah Packaging (Private) Limited and another
Khairullah Paper and Board Works (Private) Limited and others
APPELLANTS BY: M/s Saad M. Hashmi, Saeed Hassan Khan
and Rais Mahmood Ali, Advocates in
Mr. Waqas Amir, Advocate in C.M.A No.
RESPONDENTS BY: Mr. Muhammad Ahsan Bhoon, Advocate
Mr. Shafqat Mehmood Chohan and Mr.
Wasi Ullah khan Surrani, Advocates for

body: AYYAZ SHAUKAT, J:- This judgment shall dispose of C.M.A. No.28 of 2026 and C.M.A. No.29 of 2026, both filed under section 70(13) of the Anti- C.M.A Nos. 28 & 29 of 2026 Page 2 of 64 Dumping Duties Act, 2015 (the "Act"), against the judgment dated 04.05.2026 passed by the Anti-Dumping Appellate Tribunal (the "Tribunal") in Appeal No.519 of 2022. By the impugned judgment, the Tribunal, by a majority of two to one, set aside the report dated 24.08.2022 issued by the National Tariff Commission (the "Commission") upon conclusion of a sunset review, along with the consequential notice dated 25.08.2022, whereby anti-dumping duties on imports of Coated Bleached Paperboard from China had been continued for a further period of five years. C.M.A. No.28 of 2026 has been filed by two domestic producers of the product, whereas C.M.A. No.29 of 2026 has been filed by the Commission.

2. Briefly stated, the facts giving rise to these appeals are that appellant No.2 in C.M.A. No.28 of 2026, M/s Century Paper and Board Mills Limited, submitted an application to the Commission on 21.12.2015 seeking an investigation into dumped imports of Coated Bleached Paperboard (one side coated folding box board with white back) originating from China. Pursuant thereto, the Commission initiated an investigation on 08.02.2016 and made its preliminary determination on 28.02.2017. Subsequently, through its final determination notified in April 2018, the Commission imposed definitive antidumping duties ranging from 28.74% to 29.02% for a period of five years, with effect from 28.02.2017. On 23.11.2021, the Commission published a notice of impending expiry under section 58(2) of the Act. Thereafter, the two appellants, representing the domestic industry, submitted an application on 06.01.2022 seeking a sunset review. The Commission initiated the review on 25.02.2022, covering the period from 01.10.2018 to 30.09.2021. During the review proceedings, the Chinese exporters did not respond to the questionnaires issued by the Commission, which consequently proceeded on the basis of the best information available under section 32 of the Act. Upon conclusion of the review, the Commission issued its report dated 24.08.2022, determining that expiry of the existing duties would be likely to lead to recurrence of dumping and injury. Accordingly, through notice dated 25.08.2022, the Commission continued the anti-dumping duties for a further period of five years, with effect from 28.02.2022.

C.M.A Nos. 28 & 29 of 2026 Page 3 of 64 3. Respondents No.3 and 4 in C.M.A. No.28 of 2026, namely M/s Khairullah Paper and Board Works (Private) Limited and M/s Pakistan Packages (Private) Limited, being importers of the product, challenged the aforesaid report and consequential notice before the Tribunal in September 2022. The appeal was heard on various dates between December 2022 and April 2026. During the proceedings, the appeal was adjourned sine die on two occasions at the request of learned counsel for the importers. The first adjournment was sought to enable the importers to approach the Commission for a review on change of circumstances under section 59 of the Act, whereas the second was sought to await the decision in C.M.A. No.26 of 2023, filed before this Court against the original final determination. The domestic industry raised no objection to either request. The importers were also permitted to file an amended memorandum of appeal. Upon conclusion of the proceedings, the Tribunal, by a majority of two to one, allowed the appeal through its judgment dated 04.05.2026 and set aside the Commission's report dated 24.08.2022 and consequential notice dated 25.08.2022. Hence, the present appeals.

Submissions of learned counsel for the parties 4. Mr. Saad Mumtaz Hashmi, learned ASC for the appellants in C.M.A. No.28 of 2026, contends that sub-sections (5) and (6) of section 70 of the Act are mandatory and require the Tribunal to decide an appeal "not later than forty-five days" and to hear it from day to day. He submits that, since the Tribunal pronounced its judgment after approximately three years and eight months, the judgment is a nullity. In support, he relies upon Collector of Sales Tax, Gujranwala and others v. Messrs Super Asia Mohammad Din and Sons and others (2017 SCMR 1427), Province of Punjab through Conservator of Forest, Faisalabad and others v. Javed Iqbal (2021 SCMR 328), Shaheen Merchant v. Federation of Pakistan/National Tariff Commission and others (2021 PTD 2126) and Zahid Hussain v. National Tariff Commission (2025 PTD 1532). Learned counsel acknowledges that Commissioner Inland Revenue v. Sarwaq Traders (2022 SCMR 1333) was recalled on review in Commissioner Inland Revenue, Zone-III, RTO, Rawalpindi and others v. Messrs Sarwaq Traders, Rawalpindi and others (2025 C.M.A Nos. 28 & 29 of 2026 Page 4 of 64 SCMR 341), but maintains that the larger Bench in Messrs WAK Limited Multan Road, Lahore and others v. Collector Central Excise and Sales Tax, Lahore and others (2025 SCMR 1280) found the review judgment incorrect, rendering it per incuriam. He further argues, with reference to Ahsan Ali and others v. District Judge and others (PLD 1969 SC 167), that the prescribed period cannot be extended by consent, as limitation cannot be waived. In the alternative, he seeks remand of the importers' appeal to the Tribunal for a fresh decision. On the merits, learned counsel submits that interference by the Tribunal was permissible only if the Commission's evaluation was both biased and lacking in objectivity. He maintains that, owing to the exporters' non-cooperation, the distinction between what is "probable" and what is merely "possible" was inapplicable to an assessment based on the best information available, as recognised by the Tribunal in Appeal No.510 of 2022. He further questions the majority's reliance upon the unadopted WTO panel report in Pakistan - Anti-Dumping Measures on Biaxially Oriented Polypropylene Film from the United Arab Emirates (WT/DS538/R) (the "BOPP Report"), which remains under appeal, and upon the Tribunal's decision dated 25.09.2023 in Appeal No.544 of 2022, rendered after the Commission's report and presently under challenge before this Court. Relying upon Shehla Zia v. WAPDA (PLD 1994 SC 693) and SGS v. Pakistan (2002 SCMR 1694), he submits that unincorporated treaties do not form part of municipal law. He also argues that sections 15 and 17 of the Act do not govern a sunset review; that the matter ought, at least, to have been remanded to the Commission under the proviso to section 70(7); that the importers lacked standing before the Tribunal; and that anti-dumping duty is not penal in character, as held in Messrs Aimnaz (Pvt.) Limited v. Federation of Pakistan (2018 PTD 1966).

5. Mr. Waqas Amir, learned counsel for the Commission, supports the appellants' contentions and presses the Commission's independent appeal. He submits that a sunset review is inherently predictive and that the expression "recurrence" in section 58(3) of the Act necessarily contemplates a situation in which dumping and injury may have ceased during the operation of the duty. According to learned counsel, the majority of the Tribunal erroneously insisted C.M.A Nos. 28 & 29 of 2026 Page 5 of 64 upon proof of present dumping and injury, thereby treating the effectiveness of the existing duty as a reason for its discontinuation. He points out that dumped imports had not ceased altogether and continued to account for 11% of imports during the final year of review. He further refers to the increase in Chinese exports and production capacity and submits that Table-VII of the Commission's report demonstrated that, even without the anti-dumping duty, the landed cost of Chinese imports remained below the domestic selling price. He seeks to distinguish Appeal No.544 of 2022 on the ground that imports in that case had declined to zero, and the BOPP case on the ground that the exporters had cooperated with the investigating authority. Learned counsel characterises the findings recorded by the majority as an afterthought. Regarding the objection to the Commission's standing, he argues that section 70(13) does not restrict the right of appeal to an "aggrieved person" and that the Commission is expressly recognised as a statutory party under sub-sections (7), (10) and (11) of section 70. In support, he relies upon the judgment of the Hon’ble Federal Constitutional Court in M/s DG Khan Cement Company Limited v. Federation of Pakistan (C.A. No.1243 of 2020), while seeking to distinguish Wafaqi Mohtasib Secretariat, Islamabad v. SNGPL, Lahore (PLD 2020 SC 586) and A. Rahim Foods (Pvt.) Limited v. K&N's Foods (Pvt.) Limited (PLD 2023 SC 516).

6. Conversely, Mr. Feisal Hussain Naqvi, learned ASC for respondent No.3, contends that the period prescribed under section 70(5) of the Act is directory rather than mandatory. He argues that a litigant cannot be prejudiced by the failure of an adjudicatory forum to decide a matter within the prescribed period and that the statutory right of appeal cannot be extinguished on that account. Reliance is placed upon A.J. Traders v. Collector of Customs (Adjudication), Islamabad (PLD 2022 SC 817) and the review judgment in Sarwaq Traders. Learned counsel submits that WAK Limited affirmed the principle laid down in A.J. Traders and did not overrule the review judgment in Sarwaq Traders, whereas Super Asia and Javed Iqbal concerned original adjudicatory proceedings rather than appellate jurisdiction. He further maintains that the appellants participated in the proceedings before the Tribunal without raising any objection regarding delay and cannot subsequently challenge its jurisdiction on that C.M.A Nos. 28 & 29 of 2026 Page 6 of 64 ground, placing reliance upon WAPDA v. Khanzada Muhammad Abdul Haque Khan Khattak and Co. (PLD 1990 SC 359). He also opposes remand, submitting that it would merely return the controversy to the same Tribunal. On the merits, learned counsel argues that the appeal before the Tribunal is a full statutory appeal before a specialised forum. He maintains that the standard adopted by the majority had already been recognised in adopted WTO Appellate Body reports long before the BOPP Report and is now reflected in rules 40 and 41 of the Anti-Dumping Duties Rules, 2022. Relying upon Malik Asad Ali v. Federation of Pakistan (PLD 1998 SC 161) and Mir Muhammad Khan v. Haider (PLD 2020 SC 233), he submits that judicial decisions declare the existing law and that the subsequent date of the Tribunal's decision in Appeal No.544 of 2022 is consequently immaterial. He further contends that the Commission failed to determine normal value, included products outside the scope of the review in Table-V, and relied upon Chinese production capacity without examining domestic demand in China. According to learned counsel, the Commission's own tables disclosed no price undercutting, depression or suppression, while reflecting a substantial increase in the profitability of the domestic industry. He maintains that the principle of best information available governs the sources of evidence upon which the Commission may rely but does not dilute the standard governing its evaluation. Lastly, relying upon Muhammad Saleem Bikiya v. Pakistan (2018 PTD 2026), he submits that anti-dumping duty is penal in character.

7. The written submissions filed on behalf of the importers by Barrister Junaid Ahmed, and by Mr. Qasim Wadud and Mr. Saad Shuaib Wyne, learned ASCs for respondent No.5, substantially support the foregoing contentions. Learned counsel submit that an appeal under section 70(13) of the Act is confined to questions of law and does not permit this Court to undertake a fresh appraisal of evidence already examined by the Commission and the Tribunal. In this regard, they rely upon Sohail and Company v. Anti-Dumping Appellate Tribunal, Islamabad (2024 PTD 872), Dawn Convertec SMC (Pvt.) Ltd. v. National Tariff Commission (2025 PTD 724) and M/s Hamdam Paper Products (Pvt.) Limited v. National Tariff Commission (F.A.O. No.40 of 2020, decided on 28.01.2025). They further submit that sub-sections (8) and (9) of section 70 C.M.A Nos. 28 & 29 of 2026 Page 7 of 64 reproduce Article 17.6(i) of the Anti-Dumping Agreement and that confirmation of the Commission's determination is impermissible where any of the prescribed conditions remains unsatisfied. Regarding limitation, they contend that the fortyfive-day period under section 70(5) is directory, referring to the interpretation adopted by this Court in Aimnaz (supra) concerning sections 36 and 39 of the Act. They argue that, if the provision were construed as mandatory, the same interpretation would necessarily extend to the ninety-day period prescribed for disposal of appeals by this Court. Learned counsel also seek to distinguish the authorities relied upon by the appellants on the ground that those cases concerned original adjudication under fiscal statutes. On the factual aspects, they maintain that the Commission relied exclusively upon import data obtained from Pakistan Revenue Automation (Private) Limited without verifying its reliability against independent sources, as allegedly required by section 32 read with the Schedule to the Act. They further point out that Pakistan's appeal against the BOPP Report has remained unheard because the WTO Appellate Body has lacked a quorum since 11.12.2019.

8. Mr. Shafqat Mehmood Chohan, learned ASC, in the skeleton arguments and paper book filed on behalf of respondent No.5 and other importers, similarly contends that the time limits prescribed under section 70 of the Act are directory and that the authorities relied upon by the appellants concern original adjudication of tax liability. He further argues that the Commission, being a neutral investigating forum, cannot claim the status of an aggrieved person merely because its determination has been set aside. In support, he relies upon Wafaqi Mohtasib and A. Rahim Foods (supra). Referring to section 57 of the Act, learned counsel submits that an anti-dumping duty may remain in force only for so long as it is necessary to counteract dumping causing injury, and that termination is the ordinary statutory consequence while continuation constitutes an exception requiring justification. He maintains that, since the Act does not expressly prescribe the methodology for determining likelihood under section 58(3), guidance may properly be drawn from WTO jurisprudence interpreting Article 11.3 of the Anti-Dumping Agreement. In this regard, he relies upon United States - Anti-Dumping Duty on DRAMS from Korea (WT/DS99/R), United C.M.A Nos. 28 & 29 of 2026 Page 8 of 64 States - Sunset Review of Anti-Dumping Duties on Corrosion-Resistant Carbon Steel Flat Products from Japan (WT/DS244/AB/R), United States - Sunset Reviews of Anti-Dumping Measures on Oil Country Tubular Goods from Argentina (WT/DS268/AB/RW), and the BOPP Report. According to learned counsel, these authorities require the likelihood of continuation or recurrence of dumping and injury to be established as a probability rather than a mere possibility, upon positive evidence instead of assumption, and that this principle applies irrespective of the particular facts of a review. He further submits that section 32, read with paragraph 7 of the Schedule, obliged the Commission to verify the information relied upon against independent sources. He contends that the Commission recorded conclusions upon each of the four factors examined in its report without undertaking an objective evaluation of the supporting material. He also points out that the online information relied upon by the Commission was accessed on 11.02.2022, before initiation of the sunset review on 25.02.2022, and that the underlying publications were dated 30.01.2018, 16.03.2020 and 15.06.2020. Mr. Muhammad Ahsan Bhoon, learned ASC for respondents No.6 to 8, adopts the foregoing submissions.

9. In rebuttal, Mr. Saad Mumtaz Hashmi submits that the delay was caused by the importers themselves that a mere absence of objection to adjournments is not acquiescence, and that section 70(5) casts a duty on the Tribunal which the parties cannot enlarge.
10. I have heard learned counsel for the parties and have perused the record with their assistance.
PART I: PRELIMINARY QUESTIONS OF LAW (i) Whether the time limit prescribed under section 70(5) of the Act for disposal of an appeal by the Tribunal is mandatory or directory?

11. The preliminary objection concerning the validity of the impugned judgment raises a question of considerable legal significance, as it directly concerns the jurisdiction of the Appellate Tribunal to pronounce its decision after the expiry of the period prescribed under section 70(5) of the Act. The determination of this question is fundamental to the adjudication of the present C.M.A Nos. 28 & 29 of 2026 Page 9 of 64 appeals. If the statutory period of forty-five days constitutes an absolute limitation upon the Tribunal's jurisdiction, any decision rendered thereafter would be without lawful authority, and the examination of the remaining questions would become unnecessary. It is, therefore, appropriate to address this objection at the outset. Admittedly, no such objection was raised before the Tribunal during the pendency of the proceedings. Nevertheless, the objection concerns the interpretation of a statutory provision and its effect upon the jurisdiction of a judicial forum. Being a pure question of law, capable of determination on the admitted record without requiring any further factual inquiry, it may be entertained even when raised for the first time in appeal. The relevant statutory framework is contained in sub-sections (5), (6) and (13) of section 70 of the Act, which provide as follows:

(5) Such an appeal shall be disposed of and the decision of the Appellate Tribunal pronounced, as expeditiously as possible as but [sic] not later than forty-five from the date of receipt of an appeal compliant with the requirements contained in this Act.

(6) The Appellate Tribunal shall hear the appeal from day-to-day. (13) The decision of the Appellate Tribunal shall be appealable in the High Court. The High Court shall render a decision within ninety days of receiving an appeal from the decision of the Appellate Tribunal: It is undisputed that the Tribunal pronounced the impugned judgment considerably beyond the prescribed period of forty-five days. The controversy, therefore, is not whether the statutory timeframe was observed, but whether its non-observance deprived the Tribunal of jurisdiction and rendered its subsequent decision a nullity. For the reasons discussed hereinafter, I am of the considered view that the period prescribed under section 70(5) is directory in character and that its expiry does not extinguish the Tribunal's jurisdiction to determine an appeal otherwise lawfully instituted before it.

12. The distinction between mandatory and directory statutory provisions is well established in our jurisprudence. The controlling consideration is not merely the grammatical form of the provision or the use of imperative language, but the C.M.A Nos. 28 & 29 of 2026 Page 10 of 64 intention of the legislature, as gathered from the language employed, the purpose sought to be achieved, the statutory scheme as a whole, and the legal consequences that would follow from compliance or non-compliance. In Collector of Sales Tax, Gujranwala and others v. Messrs Super Asia Mohammad Din and Sons and others (2017 SCMR 1427), the Hon’ble Supreme Court explained the governing principle in the following terms:

"6. The ultimate test to determine whether a provision is mandatory or directory is that of ascertaining the legislative intent. While the use of the word 'shall' is not the sole factor which determines the mandatory or directory nature of a provision, it is certainly one of the indicators of legislative intent. Other factors include the presence of penal consequences in case of non-compliance, but perhaps the clearest indicator is the object and purpose of the statute and the provision in question. It is the duty of the Court to garner the real intent of the legislature as expressed in the law itself."

The same principle was reaffirmed in Province of Punjab through Conservator of Forest, Faisalabad and others v. Javed Iqbal (2021 SCMR 328), wherein the Hon’ble Supreme Court observed that the intention of the legislature "is to be ascertained not only from the phraseology of the provision but also by considering its nature, its object, and the consequences which would follow from construing it one way or the other". The Court further explained that "a provision in a statute is mandatory if the omission to follow it renders the proceedings to which it relates illegal and void, while a provision is directory if its observance is not necessary to the validity of the proceeding." These pronouncements establish that the classification of a statutory requirement cannot be undertaken in isolation from its legislative context. The decisive inquiry is whether the legislature intended compliance with the prescribed requirement to constitute a condition essential to the validity of the proceedings, or whether the requirement was designed to regulate the manner and expedition with which an otherwise lawful jurisdiction is to be exercised.

13. Examined solely from the standpoint of its language, section 70(5) undoubtedly conveys a sense of imperative obligation. The legislature has employed the word "shall" and has further stipulated that an appeal is to be C.M.A Nos. 28 & 29 of 2026 Page 11 of 64 disposed of "not later than" the prescribed period. Such expressions ordinarily indicate that compliance is expected and that the statutory direction is not to be treated as optional. Indeed, in Javed Iqbal (supra), the Hon’ble Supreme Court observed that negative expressions may ordinarily impart a mandatory character to a provision, even in the absence of an expressly prescribed penalty for noncompliance. That proposition, however, does not conclude the present inquiry. The legal effect of a statutory timeframe depends equally upon the nature of the function to be performed and whether the prescribed period operates as a limitation upon the existence of jurisdiction or merely regulates its exercise. This distinction was expressly recognized in Javed Iqbal (supra), wherein the Hon’ble Supreme Court observed:

"6. ... According to Sutherland; where a public officer is directed by a statute to perform a duty within a specified time, the provision as to time are only directory. This general principle, however, does not apply where the phraseology of the provision, or the nature of the act to be performed, or the consequence of performing or failing to perform it within the prescribed timeframe is such that the prescription of timeframe is actually a limitation on the power of the public functionary. Or where a public functionary is empowered to create liability against a citizen only within the prescribed time, the performance of such a duty within the specified timeframe is mandatory."

The distinction articulated in the foregoing passage is of particular relevance to the present controversy. Section 70(5) does not prescribe a period within which the Commission may initiate proceedings, impose anti-dumping duties, or otherwise create a liability against an affected person. Rather, it regulates the timeframe within which an appellate forum is required to determine a challenge to an existing determination of the Commission. The jurisdiction of the Tribunal is invoked by the institution of an appeal in accordance with the Act, and the prescribed period governs the performance of its adjudicatory function. The provision does not expressly declare that the Tribunal's jurisdiction shall cease upon the expiry of forty-five days. Nor does it make the continued existence of that jurisdiction conditional upon the appeal being decided within that period. This distinction also explains why the decisions in Javed Iqbal, Super Asia and C.M.A Nos. 28 & 29 of 2026 Page 12 of 64 Messrs WAK Limited Multan Road, Lahore and others v. Collector Central Excise and Sales Tax, Lahore and others (2025 SCMR 1280) cannot be applied mechanically to section 70(5). Those cases concerned statutory limitations upon the exercise of original powers affecting the rights or liabilities of individuals. In Javed Iqbal, the question related to the power to conclude disciplinary proceedings against a retired employee, whereas Super Asia and WAK Limited concerned the authority of revenue officials to make original adjudicatory orders within prescribed periods. In each instance, the timeframe was examined in relation to the State's power to determine or impose a liability. The present provision, by contrast, concerns the expeditious disposal of an appeal already pending before a duly constituted appellate forum. The distinction is substantive rather than merely procedural, because invalidating an original order made beyond a jurisdictional deadline protects the person against the belated exercise of State power, whereas invalidating an appellate decision solely on account of delay may deprive that very person of the statutory remedy provided against such power. The broader principle was recognized by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Dr. Habib ur Rahman v. West Pakistan Public Service Commission, Lahore and others (PLD 1973 SC 144), wherein the following passage from Maxwell on the Interpretation of Statutes (1962 Edition, page 369) was adopted: "... where the prescriptions of a statute relate to the performance of a public duty, and where the invalidation of acts done in neglect of them would work serious general inconvenience or injustice to persons who have no control over those entrusted with the duty, yet not promote the essential aims of the Legislature, such prescriptions seem to be generally understood as mere instructions for the guidance and government of those on whom the duty is imposed, or, in other words, as directory only ..."

The Court also drew support from Montreal Street Railway Company v. Normandin (AIR 1917 PC 142). The principle is directly relevant here. Although the parties may, through their conduct, contribute to the delay in appellate proceedings, the ultimate statutory responsibility to regulate the proceedings and pronounce the decision rests with the Tribunal. To invalidate its decision merely because that responsibility was not discharged within the prescribed period C.M.A Nos. 28 & 29 of 2026 Page 13 of 64 would expose the litigants to the consequences of a default over which they do not exercise exclusive control. Such an interpretation would neither advance the purpose of the appellate remedy nor secure the legislative objective of expeditious adjudication. A comparable approach has been adopted by the Supreme Court of India in C. Bright v. District Collector and others ((2021) 2 SCC 392), while interpreting the provisos to section 14 of the Securitization and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002. The statutory provision required the District Magistrate to decide an application by a secured creditor within thirty days, extendable to sixty days. Upon examining the nature of the statutory duty and the consequences of delay, the Court held that the prescribed timeframe was directory and observed: "12. ... it is a well-settled principle that if an act is required to be performed by a private person within a specified time, the same would ordinarily be mandatory but when a public functionary is required to perform a public function within a time-frame, the same will be held to be directory unless the consequences therefor are specified."

The Court further recognized that the secured creditor "has no control over the District Magistrate". The same consideration applies, with equal force, to litigants whose appeals await determination by a statutory tribunal. The principle emerging from these authorities is that a statutory direction requiring a public forum to perform an adjudicatory duty within a specified period must be construed with particular regard to whether the legislature intended delay to defeat the rights of those for whose benefit the forum was established. In the absence of a clear legislative intention to that effect, a provision intended to secure timely performance of a public duty ought not to be converted into an instrument for extinguishing the substantive rights of litigants.

14. The distinction between original adjudication and appellate adjudication has received express recognition from the Hon’ble Supreme Court in A.J. Traders v. Collector of Customs (Adjudication), Islamabad (PLD 2022 SC 817). In that case, the Court examined section 194-B of the Customs Act, 1969, which required the Customs Appellate Tribunal to decide an appeal within sixty days or within such extended period as the Tribunal might determine. The question was C.M.A Nos. 28 & 29 of 2026 Page 14 of 64 whether an appellate decision pronounced beyond the statutory timeframe was rendered void merely by reason of such delay. The Hon’ble Supreme Court answered that question in the negative, holding in paragraph 8 that "it cannot be stated that an order belatedly passed on a taxpayer's appeal is a void order and/or a nullity". The distinction underlying that conclusion was explained in the following terms:

"9. ... Belatedly adjudicating a show cause notice is not the same as belatedly deciding an appeal preferred against a purported liability, because then the appellate authority's tardiness, whether intentional or otherwise, will frustrate the taxpayer's appeal, which is not the intention of the law, nor could it be as it would violate Articles 4 and 10A of the Constitution.

10. ... The Legislature in prescribing a period within which an appeal should, or must, be decided obligates the appellate authority. Therefore, if there are any consequences in deciding an appeal beyond the prescribed period the same may only be visited upon the State functionaries, and not on an appellant taxpayer."

The reasoning is particularly instructive because it identifies the essential difference between a statutory limitation imposed upon the creation of liability and a timeframe prescribed for the determination of an appeal against that liability. In the former situation, the expiry of the prescribed period may operate as a restriction upon the authority of the State to act. In the latter, the legislature has provided an appellate remedy for the protection of an aggrieved person, and the failure of the appellate forum to discharge its duty within time cannot ordinarily be construed as extinguishing that remedy. To hold otherwise would permit the failure of the adjudicatory machinery itself to defeat a substantive right which the legislature intended to secure. The same principle was subsequently affirmed by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in its review judgment in Commissioner Inland Revenue, Zone-III, RTO, Rawalpindi and others v. Messrs Sarwaq Traders, Rawalpindi and others (2025 SCMR 341), while examining the provisos to section 45B(2) of the Sales Tax Act, 1990. The majority held that "lapse of the statutory timeframe will not affect the proceedings before the Commissioner (Appeals) who shall conclude the appeal in accordance with law by deciding the appeal on its merits." The significance of this C.M.A Nos. 28 & 29 of 2026 Page 15 of 64 pronouncement lies in its recognition that the statutory obligation of timely disposal remains enforceable without rendering the appellate proceedings invalid upon expiry of the prescribed period. A comparable consideration informed the decision of the Supreme Court of India in Deputy Commissioner of Income Tax and another v. Pepsi Foods Limited ((2021) 7 SCC 413). The third proviso to section 254(2A) of the Income Tax Act, 1961 contemplated the vacation of a stay granted by the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal if the appeal remained undecided beyond three hundred and sixty-five days, even where the delay was not attributable to the assessee. The Court held that the provision, insofar as it operated against an assessee who had not occasioned the delay, was "manifestly arbitrary being a provision which is capricious, irrational and disproportionate so far as the assessee is concerned". It accordingly construed the provision so that the stay would lapse only where the delay was attributable to the assessee. Although that case concerned the continuation of interim protection rather than the validity of an appellate decision, the underlying principle is materially relevant: the failure of an appellate forum to act within the prescribed period ought not, without sufficient legislative justification, to prejudice a litigant who has not caused that failure. The decisions in A.J. Traders and Sarwaq Traders provide direct support for applying that principle to the present controversy.

15. The reliance placed by learned counsel for the appellants upon Messrs WAK Limited Multan Road, Lahore and others v. Collector Central Excise and Sales Tax, Lahore and others (2025 SCMR 1280) requires closer examination, particularly in view of the submission that the larger Bench had departed from the reasoning adopted in the review judgment in Sarwaq Traders. It is correct that the larger Bench reaffirmed the principle laid down in Super Asia concerning statutory time limits governing original adjudication. However, the judgment does not support the further proposition that the distinction between original and appellate adjudication has been displaced. On the contrary, while considering A.J. Traders, the larger Bench expressly observed in paragraph 30 that the decision was "unexceptionable in the facts and circumstances of that case, and the statutory provisions involved", because "it was concerned with the appellate jurisdiction of the Tribunal ... and not the adjudicatory (i.e., first instance) C.M.A Nos. 28 & 29 of 2026 Page 16 of 64 jurisdiction of the concerned officer. As correctly noted by the Court different considerations applied and were relevant in the exercise of appellate jurisdiction." Far from undermining the distinction upon which the present case turns, these observations recognise its continuing significance.

16. The position concerning the review judgment in Sarwaq Traders is equally clear. The larger Bench observed in paragraph 34 that its findings "could be regarded as open for reconsideration", but expressly qualified that observation by stating that "the correctness or otherwise of the view that ultimately prevailed in that litigation is not the question before us." The legal consequence of this qualification cannot be overlooked. An observation that a particular judgment may warrant reconsideration is materially different from a determination that the judgment is incorrect or no longer represents the law. The larger Bench deliberately refrained from deciding that question. Its observations must, therefore, be understood within the limits expressly indicated in the judgment itself.

17. The distinction between a binding declaration of law and an observation not intended to determine the question under consideration is recognised in Article 189 of the Constitution. In Justice Khurshid Anwar Bhinder and others v. Federation of Pakistan and another (PLD 2010 SC 483), a fourteen-member Bench of the Hon’ble Supreme Court explained:

"... Where the Supreme Court deliberately and with the intention of settling the law, pronounces upon a question, such pronouncement is the law declared by the Supreme Court within the meaning of this Article and is binding on all Courts in Pakistan. It cannot be treated as mere obiter [dictum]. Even obiter [dictum] of the Supreme Court, due to the high place which the Court holds in the hierarchy of courts in the country, enjoy a highly respected position as if it contains a definite expression of the Court's view on a legal principle, or the meaning of a law. ..." The observations in WAK Limited are undoubtedly entitled to the highest respect. They cannot, however, be treated as having overruled a decision whose correctness the larger Bench expressly declined to determine. 20. The legislative object underlying sub-sections (5) and (6) of section 70 provides a further, and particularly compelling, indication of their intended operation. An anti-dumping determination has immediate consequences for the commercial interests of the parties affected by it. Where the Commission imposes or continues an anti-dumping duty, importers remain subject to the resulting fiscal burden upon the importation of the investigated product. Conversely, where the Commission declines to impose or continue such a duty, the domestic industry may remain exposed to imports which it alleges are being dumped and are causing injury. The practical significance of prompt appellate review is heightened by section 70(16), which provides that "a determination of the Commission shall be given full force and effect during the pendency of any appeal of such determination." The statutory determination, therefore, continues to operate while its legality and factual foundation are under appellate examination.

21. It is against this background that the requirement of expeditious disposal must be understood. The legislature prescribed a short period of forty-five days and required hearings from day to day because prolonged appellate proceedings may perpetuate the consequences of a determination which is ultimately found to be unlawful or unjustified. The provision is intended to secure an effective and timely appellate remedy, not to restrict access to that remedy by making its continued existence dependent upon the speed with which the Tribunal performs C.M.A Nos. 28 & 29 of 2026 Page 19 of 64 its functions. This legislative purpose is also consistent with the international obligations which the Act seeks to implement. Article 13 of the Anti-Dumping Agreement provides:

"Article 13 Judicial Review Each Member whose national legislation contains provisions on antidumping measures shall maintain judicial, arbitral or administrative tribunals or procedures for the purpose, inter alia, of the prompt review of administrative actions relating to final determinations and reviews of determinations within the meaning of Article 11. Such tribunals or procedures shall be independent of the authorities responsible for the determination or review in question."

The requirement of prompt and independent review embodied in Article 13 is reflected in section 70 of the Act. In particular, section 70(1)(iii) expressly permits an appeal against "any final determination pursuant to a review", thereby bringing sunset determinations within the appellate mechanism. The legislative objective is consequently twofold: to provide an independent forum capable of examining the Commission's determinations and to ensure that such examination is undertaken without avoidable delay. Neither objective would be advanced by holding that the Tribunal loses jurisdiction merely because it has failed to pronounce its decision within the prescribed period. Such a construction would transform a safeguard designed to protect the parties into a limitation capable of depriving them of the very protection for which it was enacted.

22. The consequences of the contrary interpretation illustrate the difficulty. If every appellate decision pronounced after forty-five days were void, the determination of the Commission would continue to operate under section 70(16) without an effective appellate determination, subject to the statutory limits governing the duration of the duty. An importer challenging an unlawful duty could thus remain burdened by that determination because the appellate forum failed to decide the appeal within time. Equally, the domestic industry could be deprived of an effective determination of its challenge where the Commission had declined to continue protective measures. In either situation, the statutory remedy would become vulnerable to the conduct or administrative limitations of C.M.A Nos. 28 & 29 of 2026 Page 20 of 64 the forum entrusted with its exercise. Such a consequence is difficult to reconcile with the purpose of section 70 or with the requirement of effective appellate review.

23. The structure of the Act reinforces this conclusion. Section 70(5) does not prescribe any consequence for failure to decide an appeal within forty-five days. It does not provide that the appeal shall stand allowed, dismissed or abated upon expiry of that period. Nor does it contemplate the automatic transfer of the proceedings to another forum or prescribe any alternative mechanism for their determination. If the period were treated as an absolute jurisdictional limitation, the Tribunal would cease to possess authority on the forty-sixth day, leaving the appeal neither determined nor capable of determination by that forum. The substantive right conferred upon "any interested party" under section 70(1) would consequently be defeated by the failure of the adjudicatory institution to comply with its own statutory obligation.

It is the duty of the Courts to try to get at the real intention of the Legislature, by carefully attending to the whole scope of the statute to be construed. As a general rule however, a statute is understood to be directory when it contains matter merely of direction, but not when those directions are followed up by an express provision that, in default of following them, the [acts] shall be null and void. No express provision in section 70(5), or elsewhere in the Act, declares that a decision pronounced after the prescribed period shall be void. Although the absence of such a consequence is not invariably conclusive, it assumes considerable importance when read with the nature of the right sought to be protected. The right of appeal is a substantive statutory right, and its significance has repeatedly been recognised by the superior courts. In United Bank Limited and others v. "9. It is a well settled exposition of law that a right of appeal is a right of entering into a superior court and invoking its aid and interposition to redress the error of the forum below. It is essentially a continuation of the original proceedings as a vested right of the litigant to avail the remedy of an appeal provided for appraisal and testing the soundness of the decisions and proceedings of the courts below. It is always explicated and elucidated that the right of appeal is not a mere matter of procedure but is a substantive right. ..."

The principle assumes particular importance where the alleged defect arises not from the failure of a litigant to institute proceedings in accordance with law, but from the subsequent delay of the forum before which those proceedings are pending. The statutory right of appeal cannot ordinarily be construed as becoming ineffective merely because the institution responsible for its determination has failed to comply with a direction concerning the time of disposal.

25. When section 70(5) is examined against these principles, its purpose becomes sufficiently clear. It imposes a binding obligation upon the Tribunal to dispose of appeals expeditiously, but does not make the continued existence of appellate jurisdiction dependent upon compliance with the prescribed period. The provision regulates the performance of a public adjudicatory duty and is intended to secure the effective exercise of the appellate remedy. To construe it as extinguishing jurisdiction upon expiry of forty-five days would undermine the substantive right conferred by section 70(1), defeat the objective of prompt and C.M.A Nos. 28 & 29 of 2026 Page 22 of 64 independent review, and produce consequences which the statutory scheme does not contemplate. The appropriate response to unjustified delay is to secure compliance with the statutory obligation, including through appropriate judicial directions, as recognised in Shaheen Merchant (supra), rather than to invalidate the appellate proceedings themselves.

Such an interpretation would produce the anomalous result that a litigant, having properly invoked the appellate jurisdiction of this Court, could be deprived of a decision on the merits merely because the appeal remained pending beyond the prescribed period. Nothing in the language or scheme of section 70 suggests that the legislature intended such a consequence. The use of comparable language in sub-sections (5) and (13), therefore, reinforces the conclusion that the prescribed periods are intended to secure expedition in adjudication rather than to impose an automatic limitation upon the jurisdiction of the respective appellate forums.

Where a statutory period limits the authority of a public functionary to initiate proceedings or create a liability against a citizen, considerations materially different from those governing the disposal of a pending appeal arise. 38. For the foregoing reasons, I hold that the period prescribed under section 70(5) of the Act is directory and not jurisdictional in character. (iii) The scope of an appeal under section 70(13)

I respectfully agree with the interpretation adopted in these judgments. The jurisdiction exercised by this Court under section 70(13) is essentially supervisory in its appellate character and does not contemplate a fresh examination of the entire factual controversy. Interference is warranted where the Tribunal's decision is contrary to law, where it has failed to determine a material question of law, or where a substantial procedural irregularity or legal defect has materially affected the decision on the merits. Ordinarily, a ground not urged before the Tribunal cannot be introduced for the first time in a further appeal. An exception, however, exists in respect of a pure question of law, particularly one concerning jurisdiction, which can be determined upon the existing record without requiring further investigation into disputed facts.

C.M.A Nos. 28 & 29 of 2026 Page 33 of 64 47. The relevant consideration is whether the appellate decision suffers from an error of law or a legally material defect warranting interference. Under the statutory scheme of the Act, the Commission is the investigating authority entrusted with establishing the relevant facts and making the initial determination, whereas the Tribunal is the specialized appellate forum empowered under section 70(8) and (9) to examine the propriety of those findings and the objectivity of their evaluation. This Court does not exercise the functions of either authority afresh. Its jurisdiction is confined to examining whether the Tribunal applied the correct legal principles, remained within the limits of its statutory powers, and reached its conclusions without material misreading or non-reading of the record. Where the Tribunal has properly exercised its jurisdiction and its conclusions are supported by a lawful assessment of the material, this Court cannot interfere merely because another interpretation of the same evidence may also be possible.

(iv) The objections to standing 48.
