The Commission's standing must, therefore, be examined with reference to its statutory functions and the effect of the impugned judgment upon the discharge of those functions.

49. The scheme of section 70 recognizes the Commission as a participant in the appellate proceedings. Sub-section (7) requires the Tribunal to afford the Commission and the appellant an opportunity of being heard, while sub-section (10) requires the appellate decision to contain the arguments advanced by both. Sub-section (11) further provides for communication of the decision to the respondents, including the Commission. The first proviso to section 70(13) also contemplates the Commission's participation before this Court by prohibiting the grant of an interim order against the conduct of an investigation without notice to the Commission and an opportunity of hearing. These provisions demonstrate that the legislature has accorded the Commission a distinct statutory position in proceedings concerning its determinations. In the present case, the Tribunal has annulled the Commission's report and the consequent continuation of antidumping duties. The impugned decision, therefore, directly affects the exercise of the statutory mandate entrusted to the Commission. Whether that effect is sufficient to confer standing must be considered in light of the distinction between an adjudicatory forum deciding a dispute between rival parties and a statutory authority exercising independent regulatory functions.

50. The judgments relied upon by learned counsel for the importers, namely Wafaqi Mohtasib Secretariat, Islamabad v. SNGPL, Lahore (PLD 2020 SC 586) and A. Rahim Foods (Pvt.) Limited v. K&N's Foods (Pvt.) Limited (PLD 2023 SC 516), do not, in my view, govern the present controversy. In Wafaqi Mohtasib, the Hon’ble Supreme Court held that the Ombudsman, being an independent forum entrusted with deciding complaints of maladministration, could not assume the position of a contesting party in proceedings arising from its own decisions. Similarly, in A. Rahim Foods, the Hon’ble Supreme Court examined the position of the Competition Commission of Pakistan and recognised that, although primarily a regulatory authority, it exercises quasi-judicial powers under clauses C.M.A Nos. 28 & 29 of 2026 Page 35 of 64 (a) and (d) of section 10(2) of the Competition Act, 2010 "while deciding upon the divergent claims and allegations of two competing undertakings". The Court consequently held that "an adjudicatory body deciding a matter in exercise of its quasi-judicial powers between two rival parties under a law cannot be treated as an aggrieved person if its decision is set aside or modified by a higher forum".

51. The scope of this principle was subsequently clarified by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Federal Public Service Commission v. Dr. Shumaila Naeem (PLD 2026 SC 1). The Court distinguished the position of the Federal Public Service Commission on the ground that the decision under challenge was "not a determination made in a quasi-judicial capacity … between contesting parties", and explained that A. Rahim Foods "pertains to quasi-judicial bodies seeking to defend their adjudicatory decisions". The governing distinction, therefore, lies in the character of the function performed by the statutory authority. Where an authority acts as an impartial adjudicator of a dispute between rival parties, it cannot ordinarily claim to be aggrieved merely because its decision has been reversed. Conversely, where the authority exercises an independent statutory mandate involving investigation, regulation or enforcement, the annulment of its action may directly affect the discharge of that mandate.

52. Applying this distinction, the Commission, while conducting a sunset review under section 58(3) of the Act, does not merely adjudicate a private dispute between the domestic industry and importers. Its functions are investigative and regulatory in character. The Commission is empowered to initiate a sunset review "on its own initiative", just as section 25 authorizes the initiation of an original investigation suo motu. It collects and evaluates relevant information, examines the likelihood of continuation or recurrence of dumping and injury, and determines whether the continuation of an anti-dumping duty is warranted in the public interest. Where exporters fail to cooperate, it may proceed on the basis of the best information available under the Act. The resulting determination is an exercise of statutory regulatory authority rather than the adjudication of a conventional lis between two competing parties. C.M.A Nos. 28 & 29 of 2026 Page 36 of 64 53. This distinction also finds support in Article 13 of the Anti-Dumping Agreement, reproduced in paragraph 16 above, which requires the reviewing tribunal to be independent of the authorities responsible for the determination or review under examination. The Agreement thus recognises a functional distinction between the investigating authority and the independent appellate forum. The observation in M.I. Sanitary Store v. Federation of Pakistan (PLD 2014 Lahore 583), that the Commission "exercises a quasi-judicial function in deciding the rights of the parties", was made in the context of the lawful constitution of the Commission and not in relation to its standing to challenge an appellate decision. The mere fact that the Commission's determinations affect competing commercial interests does not necessarily transform it into an adjudicatory forum deciding a dispute between rival parties.

54. The principle concerning the standing of statutory authorities has also been considered by the Hon’ble Federal Constitutional Court in D.G. Khan Cement Company Limited v. Federation of Pakistan (PLD 2026 FCC 168; 2026 PTD 625, paragraphs 119–120), wherein it was held that a public functionary entrusted with the administration of a statute may be directly aggrieved by a judgment which prevents the lawful discharge of that statutory mandate. Although the case concerned a revenue authority, the principle is relevant to the present controversy. Reference may also be made to Designated Authority (Anti- Dumping Directorate) v. Haldor Topsoe A/S ((2000) 6 SCC 626), wherein the Supreme Court of India entertained and allowed an appeal by the Designated Authority against an appellate order setting aside its anti-dumping findings, although the question of standing was not specifically examined.

55. In the present case, the impugned judgment has annulled the Commission's determination and the continuation of anti-dumping duties made pursuant to its statutory powers. The Commission is, therefore, not seeking merely to defend a decision rendered as an impartial adjudicator between rival litigants; it seeks judicial examination of an order which directly affects the exercise of its regulatory mandate. In these circumstances, the objection to its standing cannot be sustained. Even otherwise, the domestic industry, being C.M.A Nos. 28 & 29 of 2026 Page 37 of 64 directly affected by the annulment of the duties, has independently challenged the same judgment in C.M.A. No.28 of 2026, and the substantive questions raised in both appeals are identical. Accordingly, C.M.A. No.29 of 2026 is held to be maintainable, and its grounds shall be considered together with those raised in the connected appeal.

56. The objection raised by the appellants regarding the standing of the importers before the Tribunal is equally without substance. Apart from the fact that no such objection was raised during the proceedings before the Tribunal, section 70(1) of the Act expressly confers the right of appeal upon any "interested party". The definition of that expression under section 2 includes an importer of the investigated product. Respondents No.3 and 4, being importers directly affected by the continuation of anti-dumping duties, therefore possessed the requisite statutory standing to challenge the Commission's determination. The objection is, accordingly, rejected.

PART II: THE MERITS OF THE PRESENT APPEALS (i) The powers of the Tribunal 57. Having determined the preliminary objections concerning the maintainability of the appeals and the jurisdiction of the Tribunal, it is now appropriate to examine the merits of the controversy. The first question concerns the nature and extent of the appellate powers conferred upon the Tribunal under section 70 of the Act. Sub-section (7) empowers the Tribunal, after making such further inquiry as it considers necessary, to confirm, alter or annul the determination of the Commission. The exercise of these powers is, however, governed by the standards prescribed under sub-sections (8) and (9), which provide as follows:

"(8) After examining the appeal, the Appellate tribunal shall assess the facts related to the impugned determination of the Commission. The Appellate Tribunal shall determine whether the establishment of the facts of the Commission was proper and whether the commission's evaluation of those facts was unbiased and objective. The Appellate tribunal shall base this determination on the official record maintained by the C.M.A Nos. 28 & 29 of 2026 Page 38 of 64 Commission or any other documents relied upon by the Commission in reaching the determination being appealed.

(9) Where the Appellate Tribunal determines that the Commission's establishment of the facts was proper and its evaluation was unbiased and objective, it shall confirm the appealed determination of the Commission provided that the Appellate Tribunal is satisfied that in reaching its determination, the Commission complied with the relevant provisions of this Act."

58. Learned counsel for the appellants has contended that the Tribunal could interfere with the Commission's determination only upon finding that its evaluation of the facts was both biased and lacking in objectivity. This interpretation, in my view, does not accord with the language or purpose of subsections (8) and (9) of section 70. The appellants' argument proceeds upon the assumption that the statutory requirements of an unbiased and objective evaluation constitute cumulative grounds of invalidity, so that the Tribunal must establish the simultaneous existence of both defects before interfering with a determination. The statutory scheme, however, adopts a different approach. Sub-section (9) prescribes the conditions upon which the Tribunal is required to confirm a determination, rather than the circumstances in which interference alone becomes permissible.

59. A plain reading of sub-section (9) demonstrates that confirmation is conditional upon the satisfaction of three distinct requirements: first, that the Commission properly established the relevant facts; second, that its evaluation of those facts was unbiased and objective; and third, that the determination was reached in compliance with the applicable provisions of the Act. These requirements are cumulative in the sense that each must be satisfied before the statutory obligation to confirm the determination arises. Consequently, where the establishment of facts is defective, or their evaluation lacks objectivity, or the Commission has failed to comply with a relevant statutory requirement, the Tribunal is not bound to confirm the determination and may exercise the powers conferred upon it under sub-section (7), subject to the nature and materiality of the defect identified.

C.M.A Nos. 28 & 29 of 2026 Page 39 of 64 60. The words "unbiased" and "objective" describe related but distinct attributes of a lawful evaluation. An evaluation may be entirely free from personal prejudice or institutional bias and yet fail the requirement of objectivity because its conclusions are unsupported by the evidence, material circumstances have been overlooked, or the reasoning does not adequately connect the established facts with the ultimate determination. The use of the conjunction "and" does not mean that both bias and lack of objectivity must be affirmatively established before the Tribunal may interfere. Rather, it requires the Commission's evaluation to possess both qualities before confirmation becomes obligatory. In Suo Motu Case No.8 of 2018 (PLD 2019 SC 201), the Hon’ble Supreme Court observed that "in common parlance 'and' is used in the conjunctive sense, while 'or' is employed in the disjunctive sense". Relying upon Maxwell, the Court further recognised that the expressions may be construed interchangeably only "to carry out the intention of the legislature". In the present case, no departure from the ordinary conjunctive meaning is necessary. The legislature has required an evaluation which is both unbiased and objective; the absence of either quality prevents the conditions for mandatory confirmation from being fully satisfied.

61. This interpretation does not, however, authorise the Tribunal to substitute its own assessment for that of the Commission merely because another conclusion might reasonably be drawn from the same material. The Commission remains the statutory investigating authority, while the Tribunal exercises a defined appellate function. Sub-section (8) expressly confines the Tribunal's factual assessment to the official record maintained by the Commission and the documents upon which the Commission relied. The Tribunal must examine whether the facts were properly established and whether the evaluation was reasoned, unbiased and objective. It is not empowered to undertake an entirely fresh investigation or to overturn a determination merely because it would have assigned different weight to competing considerations.

62. This distinction is also reflected in Article 17.6(i) of the Anti-Dumping Agreement, upon which sub-sections (8) and (9) are substantially modelled. That C.M.A Nos. 28 & 29 of 2026 Page 40 of 64 provision expressly recognises that where the establishment of facts was proper and their evaluation was unbiased and objective, "even though the panel might have reached a different conclusion, the evaluation shall not be overturned." The statutory standard thus maintains a balance between respect for the specialised functions of the investigating authority and the necessity of effective appellate scrutiny. The Tribunal is required neither to defer unquestioningly to the Commission nor to replace its findings with its own preferred assessment. Its responsibility is to determine whether the Commission's conclusions are supported by a proper establishment and objective evaluation of the relevant facts. In the present case, the majority of the Tribunal proceeded upon the latter inquiry and concluded that the Commission's evaluation lacked the requisite objectivity. Whether that conclusion is legally sustainable must be examined in light of the governing standard and the material forming part of the Commission's record.

63. The interpretation adopted above is consistent with the approach of the WTO Appellate Body to Article 17.6(i) of the Anti-Dumping Agreement. In United States - Anti-Dumping Measures on Certain Hot-Rolled Steel Products from Japan (WT/DS184/AB/R), the Appellate Body observed that the provision "in effect defines when investigating authorities can be considered to have acted inconsistently with the Anti-Dumping Agreement". It further explained in paragraph 56 that the reviewing panel must examine whether the investigating authority properly established the relevant facts and evaluated them in an unbiased and objective manner. Where those standards have not been satisfied, the panel is required to find the establishment or evaluation of facts inconsistent with the Agreement.The nature and intensity of such review were further explained in United States - Investigation of the International Trade Commission in Softwood Lumber from Canada (Recourse to Article 21.5 of the DSU by Canada) (WT/DS277/AB/RW), wherein the Appellate Body observed: "93. ... It is well established that a panel must neither conduct a de novo review nor simply defer to the conclusions of the national authority. A panel's examination of those conclusions must be critical and searching, and be based on the information contained in the record and the C.M.A Nos. 28 & 29 of 2026 Page 41 of 64 explanations given by the authority in its published report. A panel must examine whether, in the light of the evidence on the record, the conclusions reached by the investigating authority are reasoned and adequate. ... The panel's scrutiny should test whether the reasoning of the authority is coherent and internally consistent. The panel must undertake an in-depth examination of whether the explanations given disclose how the investigating authority treated the facts and evidence in the record and whether there was positive evidence before it to support the inferences made and conclusions reached by it. The panel must examine whether the explanations provided demonstrate that the investigating authority took proper account of the complexities of the data before it, and that it explained why it rejected or discounted alternative explanations and interpretations of the record evidence. ..."

The foregoing observations provide useful guidance in understanding the standard of review embodied in section 70(8) and (9). The Tribunal is not required to conduct a de novo inquiry, nor may it accept the Commission's conclusions merely because they have been reached by a specialised investigating authority. Its scrutiny must be sufficiently rigorous to ascertain whether the Commission has considered the relevant evidence, addressed material considerations and furnished an intelligible explanation connecting the established facts with its ultimate findings. The requirement of objectivity is not satisfied by the mere reproduction of statistical information or the recording of conclusions. The reasoning must demonstrate how the available material supports the inference drawn, particularly where the determination involves an assessment of future economic consequences.

64. At the same time, the Tribunal must remain conscious of the limits of its appellate function. Where the Commission has properly established the facts, considered the relevant material and arrived at a reasoned conclusion reasonably supported by that material, the Tribunal cannot interfere merely because another conclusion may also be plausible. The balance between effective scrutiny and appropriate deference to specialised investigating authorities has also been examined by Steven P. Croley and John H. Jackson in "WTO Dispute Procedures, Standard of Review, and Deference to National Governments" ((1996) 90 American Journal of International Law 193). In my view, section 70 reflects the C.M.A Nos. 28 & 29 of 2026 Page 42 of 64 same balance by requiring meaningful examination of the Commission's reasoning while preserving its primary responsibility for investigation and factual determination.

65. The further contention that the Tribunal, instead of annulling the Commission's determination, ought to have remanded the matter for reconsideration is also without merit. Section 70(7) expressly empowers the Tribunal to confirm, alter or annul a determination, and its proviso contemplates further action by the Commission where such action is required to give effect to the Tribunal's decision. The provision does not, however, make remand an inevitable consequence of every finding of illegality or deficiency in the Commission's determination. Whether remand is appropriate must depend upon the nature of the defect identified, the relief granted and the necessity of further proceedings for implementing the appellate decision.

66. In the present case, the majority of the Tribunal annulled the continuation of anti-dumping duties upon finding that the Commission's determination regarding the likelihood of recurrence of dumping and injury was not supported by an adequate objective evaluation of the evidence. The annulment was, therefore, a substantive exercise of the appellate power expressly conferred by section 70(7). A remand could not be justified merely on the ground that the Commission might, upon reconsideration, arrive at a different or more adequately reasoned conclusion. The particular nature of a sunset review must also be kept in view. Such a review involves a forwardlooking determination made in anticipation of the expiry of an existing duty, and its statutory purpose is closely connected with that point in time. As explained by this Court in Zahid Hussain (supra), the likelihood assessment must be undertaken in the context of the approaching expiry of the duty. In the present case, that point had already passed in February 2022. In these circumstances, and having regard to the basis upon which the majority annulled the determination, no sufficient legal ground has been established for holding that the Tribunal was bound to remit the matter to the Commission. The objection is, accordingly, rejected.

C.M.A Nos. 28 & 29 of 2026 Page 43 of 64 (ii) The standard governing a sunset determination 67. The next question concerns the legal standard governing the continuation of anti-dumping duties following a sunset review under section 58(3) of the Act. The statutory scheme makes it clear that an anti-dumping duty is not intended to operate indefinitely. Section 57 provides that such duty "shall remain in force only as long as and to the extent necessary to counteract dumping, which is causing injury." Section 58(1) further requires the termination of a definitive duty not later than five years from its imposition. An exception is provided under section 58(3), which permits continuation where the Commission determines that expiry of the duty would be likely to lead to the continuation or recurrence of dumping and injury. The combined effect of these provisions is that expiry after five years is the ordinary statutory consequence, while continuation is permissible only upon a determination satisfying the conditions expressly prescribed by law.

68. The expression "likely" is central to this inquiry. It requires more than the identification of a possibility that dumping or injury may recur. The Commission must determine, upon an objective evaluation of relevant evidence, that such recurrence is probable. Both elements of the statutory test, namely dumping and injury, must be addressed. A finding concerning the likelihood of dumping, without a corresponding examination of the likelihood of injury, would not satisfy the requirements of section 58(3). Equally, the mere fact that duties were previously imposed cannot, without further examination, justify their continuation. The Commission must establish why their expiry would probably result in the continuation or recurrence of the circumstances which originally warranted their imposition.

69. The requirement of a demonstrable evidentiary foundation is also reflected in the interpretation of Article 11.3 of the Anti-Dumping Agreement. In United States - Anti-Dumping Duty on DRAMS from Korea (WT/DS99/R), the WTO panel explained:

"6.42 ... We note that the necessity of the measure is a function of certain objective conditions being in place, i.e. whether circumstances C.M.A Nos. 28 & 29 of 2026 Page 44 of 64 require continued imposition of the anti-dumping duty. That being so, such continued imposition must, in our view, be essentially dependent on, and therefore assignable to, a foundation of positive evidence that circumstances demand it. In other words, the need for the continued imposition of the duty must be demonstrable on the basis of the evidence adduced."

The five-year termination requirement introduced through Article 11.3 during the Uruguay Round was intended to impose a meaningful discipline upon the duration of anti-dumping measures. Its practical significance is reflected in the empirical study undertaken by Olivier Cadot, Jaime de Melo and Bolormaa Tumurchudur, entitled "Anti- Dumping Sunset Reviews: The Uneven Reach of WTO Disciplines", CEPR Discussion Paper No.6502, 2007. The study, examining revocations between 1979 and 2005, found that the five-year cycle of revocation became apparent following the WTO Agreement, with the marginal propensity to revoke measures at five years "jumping from 0-2% to 45%". Although such empirical material does not determine the meaning of the Act, it illustrates the importance of treating the sunset mechanism as a substantive statutory safeguard rather than a procedural formality. Section 58 must, therefore, be applied in a manner which gives meaningful effect to the legislative requirement that continuation of a duty be justified by a fresh, evidence-based assessment of its necessity.

70. The meaning of the expression "likely" in section 58(3) is further illuminated by the interpretation of the corresponding language in Article 11.3 of the Anti-Dumping Agreement. In United States - Sunset Review of Anti-Dumping Duties on Corrosion-Resistant Carbon Steel Flat Products from Japan (WT/DS244/AB/R), the WTO Appellate Body observed:

"111. ... authorities conducting a sunset review must act with an appropriate degree of diligence and arrive at a reasoned conclusion on the basis of information gathered as part of a process of reconsideration and examination. In view of the use of the word 'likely' in Article 11.3, an affirmative likelihood determination may be made only if the evidence demonstrates that dumping would be probable if the duty were terminated -and not simply if the evidence suggests that such a result might be possible or plausible."

C.M.A Nos. 28 & 29 of 2026 Page 45 of 64 The Appellate Body further observed in paragraph 113 that "authorities must conduct a rigorous examination in a sunset review before the exception (namely, the continuation of the duty) can apply." Subsequent reports, including those arising from the United States - Sunset Reviews of Anti-Dumping Measures on Oil Country Tubular Goods from Argentina dispute, have consistently emphasised that a likelihood determination must rest upon positive evidence and a sufficient factual foundation rather than assumption or conjecture. The expression "positive evidence" was explained in United States - Anti-Dumping Measures on Certain Hot-Rolled Steel Products from Japan (supra) as requiring evidence "that the evidence must be of an affirmative, objective and verifiable character, and that it must be credible."

71. A similar interpretation has been adopted by the courts of the United States. In Usinor Industeel, S.A. v. United States (Slip Op. 02-39, decided on 29.04.2002), the United States Court of International Trade held that the word "likely" bears its ordinary meaning of probable and is "nowhere defined as merely 'possible'". The matter was remanded for determination of "whether injury is likely, not just possible". These authorities are persuasive because they recognise the essential distinction between a prediction supported by objective evidence and a speculative assessment of what might occur upon the withdrawal of an existing measure.

72. The standard, however, is not dependent upon the direct application of foreign law. It arises from the language of section 58(3) itself. A determination that dumping and injury are "likely" to continue or recur necessarily requires a reasoned assessment that such consequences are probable. The predictive character of a sunset review does not dispense with the requirement of evidence; rather, it requires the Commission to draw a rational inference about future events from facts objectively established at the time of review. The conclusion need not possess mathematical certainty, but it must be supported by material capable of reasonably sustaining the prediction.

73. This Court recognized the same principle in Zahid Hussain (supra), observing that a sunset review involves an investigative and adjudicatory C.M.A Nos. 28 & 29 of 2026 Page 46 of 64 exercise founded upon positive evidence and an objective examination of existing facts. Rules 40 and 41 of the Anti-Dumping Duties Rules, 2022, although subsequently introduced and not applicable to the present review, reflect a similar approach. Significantly, both the majority and minority opinions of the Tribunal proceeded upon the requirement of a reasoned likelihood determination, and learned counsel for the Commission did not suggest that section 58(3) prescribed a different standard. The controversy, therefore, concerns the application of that standard to the Commission's determination rather than its existence.

74. The competing submissions regarding whether anti-dumping duty is penal in character, with reference to Aimnaz and Muhammad Saleem Bikiya (supra), do not require resolution for present purposes. Whether characterized as a protective fiscal measure or otherwise, its continuation remains governed by the express requirements of section 58(3). Those requirements cannot be relaxed or enlarged merely by reference to the legal character attributed to the duty.

75. The objection raised by learned counsel for the appellants regarding reliance upon WTO jurisprudence must be considered in the context of the legislative purpose of the Act. Its preamble expressly declares that the legislation has been enacted "to give effect in Pakistan to the provisions of Article VI of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, 1994, and to the Agreement on Implementation thereof". Section 58(3) substantially incorporates Article 11.3 of the Anti-Dumping Agreement, while sub-sections (8) and (9) of section 70 reflect the standard of review contained in Article 17.6(i). The present case, therefore, does not concern the direct enforcement of an unincorporated international treaty. Rather, it concerns the interpretation of domestic statutory provisions enacted to give effect to international obligations. In such circumstances, the interpretation placed upon corresponding treaty provisions by WTO panels and the Appellate Body may legitimately be considered as an aid to statutory construction. Such interpretations are not binding upon domestic courts, but may C.M.A Nos. 28 & 29 of 2026 Page 47 of 64 carry considerable persuasive weight, particularly where the statutory language closely follows the Agreement.

76. The principle that domestic legislation should, so far as its language permits, be interpreted consistently with international obligations has long been recognized in Pakistan. In Hanover Fire Insurance Company v. Muralidhar Banechand (PLD 1958 SC 138), the Hon’ble Supreme Court adopted the following passage from Maxwell on the Interpretation of Statutes (Tenth Edition, page 148):

"Under the same general presumption that the legislature does not intend to exceed its jurisdiction, every statute is to be so interpreted and applied, as far as its language admits, as not to be inconsistent with the comity of nations, or with the established rules of international law. ... But if the statute is unambiguous, its provisions must be followed, even if they are contrary to international law."

The application of this principle to legislation incorporating WTO obligations was specifically examined by the Sindh High Court in Sadia Jabbar v. Federation of Pakistan and others (2018 PTD 1746). Speaking through Munib Akhtar, J., the learned Division Bench observed:

"10. ... If it is clear that a statute or statutory provision embodies a WTO agreement, and especially where the statutory language essentially reproduces or closely follows the text of the agreement, then the interpretation should invariably be that which is consistent with the agreement and obligations thereunder. In other words, the threshold for concluding that a meaning inconsistent with the WTO agreement was intended must be regarded as higher than would be the situation in the general case. To the maximum extent possible, the relevant provision should be understood and applied in its WTO context. ..."

The same Court, while examining the present legislation in Muhammad Saleem Bikiya v. Pakistan (2018 PTD 2026), observed that "a comparison of the ADD Act and the AD Agreement shows that the former seeks to faithfully give effect to the latter." The Court also recognised the relevance of the WTO dispute settlement mechanism in understanding the obligations embodied in the Agreement. Similarly, in Commissioner Inland Revenue, Zone-IV, Karachi v. Messrs A.P. Moller Maersk and another (2024 SCMR 741), the Hon’ble Supreme Court, while C.M.A Nos. 28 & 29 of 2026 Page 48 of 64 considering the interpretation of tax treaties given effect in Pakistan, held that their provisions should be "interpreted in a common and workable manner, taking into account international tax language, legal decisions of other countries, model treaties, along with their commentaries, ... and scholarly academic works where appropriate." Although that judgment arose in the context of international taxation, the underlying principle is equally applicable where Parliament has deliberately adopted language derived from an international agreement.

77. The reliance placed upon SGS v. Pakistan (2002 SCMR 1694) is, therefore, distinguishable. In that case, the treaty had not been "incorporated through legislation into the laws of the Country", and the Hon’ble Supreme Court consequently declined to recognise its provisions as directly enforceable rights under municipal law. The present Act stands on a different footing, having been expressly enacted to implement the Anti-Dumping Agreement. Accordingly, while the interpretation of domestic law remains the responsibility of this Court, relevant WTO jurisprudence may properly be consulted to understand the meaning and application of statutory provisions which reproduce or substantially embody the Agreement.

78. This approach is also consistent with the jurisprudence of other jurisdictions administering anti-dumping legislation enacted in pursuance of international trade obligations. In National Corn Growers Association v. Canada (Import Tribunal) ([1990] 2 SCR 1324), the Supreme Court of Canada considered the interpretation of the Special Import Measures Act in the context of Canada's obligations under the GATT. Gonthier, J., speaking for the majority, observed:

"... In interpreting legislation which has been enacted with a view towards implementing international obligations, as is the case here, it is reasonable for a tribunal to examine the domestic law in the context of the relevant agreement to clarify any uncertainty. Indeed where the text of the domestic law lends itself to it, one should also strive to expound an interpretation which is consonant with the relevant international obligations. Second, and more specifically, it is reasonable to make reference to an international agreement at the very outset of the inquiry C.M.A Nos. 28 & 29 of 2026 Page 49 of 64 to determine if there is any ambiguity, even latent, in the domestic legislation. ..."

A similar principle was recognised by the Court of Justice of the European Union in Petrotub SA and Republica SA v. Council of the European Union (Case C-76/00 P, decided on 09.01.2003). The Court observed in paragraph 57 that legislation adopted to implement the Anti-Dumping Agreement "must, so far as possible, be interpreted in a manner that is consistent with international law, in particular where its provisions are intended specifically to give effect to an international agreement". Applying that principle, the Court annulled the regulation insofar as it concerned the appellants because the explanation required under Article 2.4.2 of the Agreement had not been furnished, notwithstanding the absence of an express corresponding requirement in the domestic regulation.

79. These decisions reinforce the proposition that international agreements may provide legitimate interpretative guidance where domestic legislation has been enacted to implement their provisions. They do not, however, authorise a court to disregard clear statutory language or to substitute international jurisprudence for the law enacted by Parliament. In the present case, the relevant WTO interpretations are consistent with the language and purpose of sections 58 and 70 of the Act and may, therefore, properly inform their construction.

80. The objection concerning the Tribunal's reliance upon the WTO panel report in Pakistan - Anti-Dumping Measures on Biaxially Oriented Polypropylene Film from the United Arab Emirates (WT/DS538/R), referred to as the BOPP Report, and its earlier decision in Appeal No.544 of 2022, is equally unpersuasive. In the first place, the majority did not rely upon those decisions as establishing a new legal standard. The requirement that a sunset determination be supported by positive evidence demonstrating the probability, rather than the mere possibility, of recurrence had already been recognised in adopted WTO Appellate Body reports. The distinction sought to be drawn on the basis of the different factual circumstances of those cases does not, therefore, affect the applicability of the underlying legal principle. Nevertheless, the BOPP Report C.M.A Nos. 28 & 29 of 2026 Page 50 of 64 remains an appealed and unadopted panel report, and its reasoning can be considered only for its persuasive value, without attributing to it any binding legal effect.

81. Secondly, the Commission itself had previously taken action with reference to the recommendations contained in the BOPP Report. By notice dated 16.07.2021, issued more than a year before the determination presently under challenge, the Commission terminated the anti-dumping duties on BOPP Film, stating:

"To implement the recommendation of WTO Panel regarding original investigation and first sunset review, the Commission has decided to terminate antidumping duties imposed on imports of BOPP Film originating in/and or exported from the Exporting Countries."

This circumstance does not make the panel report binding upon the Commission, nor does it prevent the Commission from questioning its legal reasoning in subsequent proceedings. It does, however, demonstrate that the report was not treated by the Commission itself as wholly irrelevant to the administration of the Act. The proper inquiry remains whether the reasoning relied upon by the Tribunal is persuasive and consistent with the applicable statutory provisions.

82. Thirdly, the fact that Appeal No.544 of 2022 was decided on 25.09.2023, after the Commission's determination dated 24.08.2022, does not render its legal reasoning irrelevant. The principles applied in that decision were derived from WTO Appellate Body reports issued in 2004 and 2007, which predated the present sunset review. Moreover, judicial interpretation ordinarily declares the meaning of an existing legal provision rather than creating a new rule merely from the date of the judgment. As explained by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Malik Asad Ali v. Federation of Pakistan (PLD 1998 SC 161), by interpreting the law, the Courts only declare the true meaning of the law which already existed. Therefore, to that extent the law declared by the Court is applicable from the date the law is enacted. In any event, the majority of the Tribunal did not rest its decision exclusively upon either the BOPP Report or Appeal No.544 of 2022. It independently examined the Commission's determination and recorded its C.M.A Nos. 28 & 29 of 2026 Page 51 of 64 findings with reference to the material available in the present review. The objection to reliance upon those authorities, therefore, does not establish any error of law warranting interference.

(iii) Non-cooperation and the best information available 83. The principal justification advanced by the Commission for its reliance upon secondary information is that the Chinese exporters did not cooperate in the sunset review. While such non-cooperation undoubtedly entitled the Commission to resort to the best information available, it did not relieve it of the obligation to make a reasoned determination under section 58(3) of the Act. Section 32, read with the Schedule to the Act, permits reliance upon secondary sources where interested parties fail to provide the requisite information. Paragraph 7 of the Schedule, however, expressly requires such information to be treated with "special circumspection" and, where practicable, verified against independent sources "such as published price lists, official import statistics and customs returns". These provisions regulate the sources and reliability of the information upon which the Commission may act; they do not dilute the substantive requirement of establishing the likelihood of continuation or recurrence of dumping and injury. With respect, insofar as Appeal No.510 of 2022 suggests otherwise, it does not correctly state the law. The same contention was considered and rejected by the Tribunal in Appeal No.544 of 2022 in the following terms:

"The plea of the respondents that they were restrained in their analysis due to non-cooperation of the exporters does not hold much ground as there are many sources from where the statistics of import/export and their prices are available."

The record of the present review demonstrates that alternative sources were available. The Commission obtained export statistics from the website of the International Trade Centre and information concerning Chinese production capacity from news reports published on various websites. In the BOPP sunset review, it had similarly relied upon Trade Map statistics and information available on producers' websites. Furthermore, during the hearing held on 18.05.2022, the C.M.A Nos. 28 & 29 of 2026 Page 52 of 64 importers specifically requested verification of the product-specific RISI (Fastmarkets) data directly from its source, notwithstanding that the domestic industry had itself relied upon that source in its application. The exporters' noncooperation did not prevent the Commission from examining the available information concerning Chinese demand, export prices or production capacity, or from assessing its reliability.

84. The corresponding provisions of the Anti-Dumping Agreement were examined by the WTO Appellate Body in Mexico - Definitive Anti-Dumping Measures on Beef and Rice (WT/DS295/AB/R), wherein it observed: "289. With respect to the facts that an agency may use when faced with missing information, the agency's discretion is not unlimited. First, the facts to be employed are expected to be the 'best information available'. In this respect, we agree with the Panel's explanation: The use of the term 'best information' means that information has to be not simply correct or useful per se, but the most fitting or 'most appropriate' information available in the case at hand. ... Secondly, when culling necessary information from secondary sources, the agency should ascertain for itself the reliability and accuracy of such information by checking it, where practicable, against information contained in other independent sources at its disposal, including material submitted by interested parties. Such an active approach is compelled by the obligation to treat data obtained from secondary sources 'with special circumspection'."

The importers' request for verification of the RISI data called for precisely such an examination. Non-cooperation may enlarge the range of information upon which the Commission can rely, but it does not dispense with the obligation to assess that information critically and establish a sufficient evidentiary foundation for its conclusions. The Commission was, therefore, required to demonstrate that its determination satisfied section 58(3), notwithstanding the absence of cooperation from the exporters.

(iv) The findings on likely dumping 85. The Commission examined four factors in assessing the likelihood of continuation or recurrence of dumping: first, whether Chinese exporters had discontinued or continued exports to Pakistan; second, whether they had C.M.A Nos. 28 & 29 of 2026 Page 53 of 64 developed alternative export markets; third, changes in their production capacity, output and inventories; and fourth, the trade-remedy measures imposed by other countries. The majority of the Tribunal concluded that the Commission's analysis of these factors did not provide an adequate evidentiary basis for its determination. Having examined the relevant findings in the light of the statutory standard discussed above, I find no error of law in that conclusion, for the reasons which follow.

86. The first factor concerned the decline in imports from China following the imposition of anti-dumping duties. Table-IV of the Commission's report recorded that imports had decreased from 57,625 metric tonnes, representing 99.6% of total imports during the original period of investigation, to 1,405 metric tonnes, representing 11% during the final year of the review. On the basis of this reduction, the Commission concluded in paragraph 24.3:

"24.3 Substantial reduction in the volume of dumped imports of Coated Bleached Paperboard from China was due to imposition of anti-dumping duties. In case antidumping duties are terminated on dumped import of Coated Bleached Paperboard from China, there is likelihood that the exporters/producers will again start dumping into Pakistan."

The difficulty with this reasoning is that it proceeds directly from the reduction in import volumes to the probability of renewed dumping without explaining the evidentiary connection between the two. The Commission assumed that the decline resulted from the duties and that their withdrawal would necessarily lead to the resumption of dumped imports. Yet the report contains no corresponding analysis of export prices or normal value capable of supporting that inference. Although imports from China had not ceased altogether, the Commission did not examine whether the prices of the consignments which continued to enter Pakistan indicated dumping, nor did it compare those prices with the normal value established during the original investigation or any other relevant benchmark.

87. A similar deficiency was identified by the WTO panel in the BOPP dispute, which observed that a reduction in imports following the imposition of duties "suggests that it is possible that the opposite could happen upon removal of the C.M.A Nos. 28 & 29 of 2026 Page 54 of 64 duties", but does not, without further reasoning, establish that such a consequence is likely. The panel described the Commission's finding as "essentially conclusory". Likewise, in Appeal No.544 of 2022, the Tribunal held that a likelihood determination made "merely on the basis of exports quantities is, therefore, based on incomplete information."

88. This does not mean that a substantial reduction in imports is irrelevant to a sunset review. Import volumes and dumping margins may constitute important indicators of future conduct. Nor does section 58(3) invariably require the calculation of a fresh dumping margin. Nevertheless, where the Commission relies principally upon the decline in import volumes, it must explain why that decline, considered alongside the available market and pricing information, makes renewed dumping probable upon termination of the duty. Paragraph 24.3 provides no such explanation. The majority of the Tribunal was, therefore, justified in finding the Commission's reasoning insufficient on this aspect.

89. The same principle was examined by the WTO Appellate Body in United States - Anti-Dumping Measures on Oil Country Tubular Goods from Mexico (WT/DS282/AB/R), where a significant decline in imports following the imposition of duties had been treated as indicating that dumping would recur upon revocation. The Appellate Body rejected the use of such a presumption as the sole basis for a likelihood determination and observed:

"199. ... A respondent party may have the responsibility to introduce relevant evidence in its favour, but the investigating authority also has a duty to seek information to ensure that its determination rests on a sufficient evidentiary foundation. An affirmative determination cannot rest merely on a presumption ... that the cessation of dumping or of imports was due solely to the anti-dumping duty order.

200. ... A company's strategy and ability to increase or decrease its exports to particular markets depend on a variety of market conditions, such as, in particular, the opportunities available in different markets and the competitive conditions in the market place. Therefore, unless all relevant factors are taken into account, there may not be an objective evaluation in such cases of the causes of the variations in import volumes in the importing Member's market."

C.M.A Nos. 28 & 29 of 2026 Page 55 of 64 The reasoning contained in paragraph 24.3 of the Commission's report suffers from substantially the same deficiency. The submission that the Tribunal effectively penalised the anti-dumping duty for having achieved its intended purpose does not answer the objection. The effectiveness of a duty in reducing imports may support its continued necessity, but it does not conclusively establish that necessity. A reduction in imports may equally reflect changes in export opportunities, domestic demand in the exporting country or other market conditions. The Commission was required to examine those possibilities before concluding that termination would probably result in renewed dumping. The remaining factors were intended to address precisely these considerations, but, as discussed below, their evaluation also disclosed material deficiencies.

90. The second factor concerned the development of alternative export markets by Chinese producers. For this purpose, the Commission relied upon Table-V, compiled from Trade Map statistics, showing Chinese exports of paperboard to different destinations. A footnote to that table expressly acknowledged that the figures included "two-sided coated bleached Paperboard/clay coated bleached paperboard", although both products had been excluded from the scope of the review under paragraph 14.1 of the same report. The Commission neither segregated the figures relating to the investigated product nor explained why the combined statistics could nevertheless provide a reliable basis for assessing its export trends.

91. A further difficulty arises from the substantial inconsistency between Tables IV and V. Whereas Table-IV recorded a decline in imports into Pakistan from China from 57,625 metric tonnes to 1,405 metric tonnes, Table-V showed Chinese exports to Pakistan decreasing from 68,736 metric tonnes to 42,515 metric tonnes. The divergence was material and required explanation, particularly because the latter table included products falling outside the scope of the review. No reconciliation of these figures was undertaken.

92. The inference drawn from Table-V is also difficult to sustain. In paragraph 25.2, the Commission observed that Chinese exports to the world had increased by approximately 1.7% and concluded that this "indicates that China has not C.M.A Nos. 28 & 29 of 2026 Page 56 of 64 developed any new markets, therefore, there is likelihood that dumped imports of Coated Bleached Paperboard from China would increase if anti-dumping duties are terminated." Yet the same table reflected substantial increases in exports to Viet Nam, the United Arab Emirates, Bangladesh and Korea. The Commission did not explain how those increases were consistent with its conclusion that alternative markets had not been developed. More importantly, it did not establish why the available export trends made a diversion of dumped exports to Pakistan probable upon termination of the duties.

93. The requirement that an investigating authority's reasoning be "coherent and internally consistent", as recognised in Softwood Lumber (supra), assumes particular importance where a determination depends upon statistical evidence. The unexplained inclusion of excluded products, the material divergence between the two tables and the absence of a reasoned connection between the export figures and the predicted recurrence of dumping undermine the objectivity of the Commission's evaluation. The majority of the Tribunal, therefore, committed no legal error in declining to accept this factor as sufficient support for the likelihood determination.

94. The third factor concerned the existence of an exportable surplus in China. This aspect disclosed a material deficiency in the Commission's analysis, particularly because paragraph 26.1 of its report expressly acknowledged: "26.1 The data for international production and demand is not available, ..."

An exportable surplus ordinarily represents production exceeding domestic demand. An increase in production capacity, without an assessment of domestic consumption, does not necessarily establish that surplus production is available for export. Nevertheless, the Commission relied principally upon information concerning capacity expansion, without examining the corresponding demand for the investigated product in China.

95. The material relied upon was itself of limited probative value. The footnotes to paragraph 26.3 reveal that the relevant websites were accessed on C.M.A Nos. 28 & 29 of 2026 Page 57 of 64 11.02.2022, before initiation of the sunset review on 25.02.2022, while the underlying publications were dated 2018 and 2020. At least one publication concerned machinery for containerboard, a product outside the scope of the review. Furthermore, the EUWID report concerning the expansion plans of APP China expressly recorded that "some other Chinese companies ... reportedly massively reduced their export volumes during the 2017 demand and price boom in China", and that the expansion project "still was in very early stages". These documents formed part of the material relied upon by the Commission and were, therefore, available for examination by the Tribunal under section 70(8).

96. The significance of these matters lies in the relationship between production capacity, domestic demand and export availability. The material itself indicated that increased domestic demand could substantially affect Chinese export volumes, yet the Commission undertook no corresponding examination of that factor. Its further conclusion in paragraph 26.4 that "the inventories of Coated Bleached Paperboard of China has increased and it has exportable surplus to dump in Pakistan" was unsupported by any identified inventory data. Although learned counsel for the importers subsequently produced market reports concerning Chinese demand, those reports were not before the Commission and have not been relied upon in reaching the present conclusion. The deficiency arises from the Commission's own record. In the absence of a reasoned assessment of domestic demand, inventories and the relevance of the capacity figures, the finding concerning an exportable surplus lacked an adequate evidentiary foundation.

97. The fourth factor concerned trade-remedy measures imposed by other countries. In paragraph 27 of its report, the Commission expressly recorded that "No country has imposed any trade remedy measures on Coated Bleached Paperboard from China during the POR." Having identified this factor as relevant to its likelihood assessment, the Commission was required to explain its significance, particularly because the recorded fact did not affirmatively support the continuation of duties. No such explanation was furnished. C.M.A Nos. 28 & 29 of 2026 Page 58 of 64 98. The absence of trade-remedy measures in other jurisdictions does not, by itself, establish that dumping into Pakistan is unlikely. To that extent, the observation of the learned Chairman of the Tribunal was correct, and the majority's treatment of this factor may have been expressed too broadly. Nevertheless, an objective evaluation requires the investigating authority to consider material circumstances which may qualify or weaken its proposed conclusion. As recognised by the WTO panel in the BOPP dispute, evidence inconsistent with an investigating authority's findings cannot simply be disregarded without explanation. The Commission's failure to address the implications of its own finding under this factor constituted a further deficiency in the reasoning supporting its likelihood determination.

99. The requirement of objectivity under section 70(8) is not satisfied merely because an investigating authority has collected information and recorded findings upon the factors selected for examination. The evaluation must demonstrate that the relevant evidence has been considered fairly and that the conclusions drawn are reasonably supported by it. In Hot-Rolled Steel (supra), the WTO Appellate Body explained that an objective examination "requires that the domestic industry, and the effects of dumped imports, be investigated in an unbiased manner, without favouring the interests of any interested party, or group of interested parties, in the investigation." Similarly, in Softwood Lumber (supra), it emphasised the obligation to explain "why it rejected or discounted alternative explanations and interpretations of the record evidence".

100. These principles require an investigating authority to consider not only material supporting the continuation of a duty but also evidence reasonably capable of supporting a different conclusion. Where material inconsistencies remain unexplained, relevant market conditions are not examined, or contrary evidence is passed over without discussion, the resulting assessment cannot readily be characterised as objective. The Commission was not required to accept every alternative explanation advanced by the interested parties. It was, however, required to demonstrate that such explanations had been considered and to provide intelligible reasons for rejecting them. That requirement assumes C.M.A Nos. 28 & 29 of 2026 Page 59 of 64 particular importance in a sunset review, where the ultimate determination concerns the probability of future events rather than the mere existence of historical circumstances.

101. The majority of the Tribunal concluded that the Commission's finding concerning the likelihood of renewed dumping rested upon assumptions regarding the consequences of terminating the duty, export statistics which included products outside the scope of the review, and production-capacity information unaccompanied by any meaningful assessment of domestic demand or inventories. These conclusions were drawn from the Commission's report and the documents upon which it had relied. The appellants have not demonstrated that the majority introduced extraneous material, materially misread the record, or disregarded evidence capable of altering its conclusions.

102. The contention that the majority's findings were an afterthought is, therefore, without substance. Section 70(8) expressly required the Tribunal to examine whether the Commission had properly established the facts and evaluated them in an unbiased and objective manner. In undertaking that examination, the majority remained within the limits of its statutory jurisdiction. Its conclusions were supported by identifiable deficiencies in the Commission's reasoning and were accompanied by reasons addressing the relevant factors. The objection founded upon section 24-A of the General Clauses Act, 1897 is consequently without merit.

103. I am, therefore, satisfied that no error of law has been established in the majority's conclusion concerning the likelihood of continuation or recurrence of dumping. Since section 58(3) requires an affirmative determination concerning the likelihood of both dumping and injury, the failure to establish the former would itself be sufficient to sustain the impugned judgment. Nevertheless, as the parties have also addressed the findings concerning likely injury, it is appropriate to examine that aspect independently.

C.M.A Nos. 28 & 29 of 2026 Page 60 of 64 (v) The findings on likely injury 104. The findings concerning the likelihood of injury lead to the same conclusion. Learned counsel for the appellants contends that the majority of the Tribunal erroneously applied sections 15 and 17 of the Act to a sunset review, although those provisions principally govern the determination of injury in an original investigation. The distinction is well founded to the extent that a sunset review does not require the Commission to establish the existence of present injury afresh. Nor does the absence of present injury necessarily justify termination of an existing anti-dumping duty, since the very purpose of that duty may have been to prevent such injury. The learned Chairman of the Tribunal correctly recognised this distinction. However, the objection overlooks the approach adopted by the Commission itself. In its notice dated 25.08.2022, the Commission expressly stated that the "factors and indices listed in Sections 15 and 17 of the Act for injury analysis have been analyzed". Having chosen to rely upon those factors in assessing the likelihood of future injury, the Commission was required to evaluate them objectively and explain how they supported its conclusion. The Tribunal was, therefore, entitled to examine whether that analysis satisfied the requirements of section 58(3). Although an isolated observation in the majority opinion may suggest that the existence of present price undercutting was treated as a prerequisite, the opinion, read as a whole, rests upon a different and legally sustainable ground: that the Commission predicted the recurrence of price undercutting, depression and suppression without adequately explaining why those consequences were probable on the basis of the available evidence.

105. The distinction between an original injury determination and a likelihoodof-injury assessment in a sunset review was examined by the WTO Appellate Body in United States - Sunset Reviews of Anti-Dumping Measures on Oil Country Tubular Goods from Argentina (WT/DS268/AB/R). The Appellate Body held that investigating authorities "are not mandated to follow the provisions of Article 3 when making a likelihood-of-injury determination". It nevertheless explained:

C.M.A Nos. 28 & 29 of 2026 Page 61 of 64 "284. This is not to say, however, that in a sunset review determination, an investigating authority is never required to examine any of the factors listed in the paragraphs of Article 3. Certain of the analyses mandated by Article 3 and necessarily relevant in an original investigation may prove to be probative, or possibly even required, in order for an investigating authority in a sunset review to arrive at a 'reasoned conclusion'. In this respect, we are of the view that the fundamental requirement of Article 3.1 that an injury determination be based on 'positive evidence' and an 'objective examination' would be equally relevant to likelihood determinations under Article 11.3. ..."

Sections 15 and 17 of the Act substantially reflect the principles contained in Article 3 of the Anti-Dumping Agreement. Accordingly, although the Commission is not required to repeat the entire exercise undertaken during an original investigation, the requirement of positive evidence and an objective evaluation remains applicable to the factors upon which it chooses to rely. The essential question is whether the available material reasonably supports the prediction that injury would continue or recur upon termination of the duty. The Tribunal was, therefore, acting within its statutory jurisdiction in examining the adequacy of the Commission's reasoning against that standard.

106. The majority's conclusion finds substantial support in the Commission's own record. Table-VII disclosed that, with the anti-dumping duty in force, there was no price undercutting. Even without the duty, the margin of undercutting had declined from 14.8% during the original period of investigation to 2.3% in the final year of the review. The Commission also recorded the absence of price depression and price suppression. At the same time, the principal indicators of the domestic industry's performance reflected considerable improvement. Its share of the domestic market had increased to 83.66%, while the share of dumped imports had declined to 1.44%. Capacity utilisation had risen from 65.61% to 83.75%, and return on investment had increased from 2.06% to 23.92%. Production, sales and cash flow had also improved, while the industry's financial performance had changed from a net loss to substantial profitability.

107. These improvements did not, by themselves, establish that injury would be unlikely to recur. They were nevertheless material circumstances requiring C.M.A Nos. 28 & 29 of 2026 Page 62 of 64 examination before an affirmative likelihood determination could properly be made. The Commission was required to explain why, notwithstanding the industry's improved position and the substantially reduced margin of potential price undercutting, termination of the duty would probably result in renewed injury. Its report did not provide an adequate explanation connecting the recorded indicators with that prediction. Instead, it proceeded substantially upon the assumption that the favourable developments observed during the operation of the duty would reverse upon its withdrawal.
108. A comparable deficiency was identified by the WTO panel in the BOPP dispute, which observed:

"7.608 ... the NTC appears to have assumed that, because dumped imports had decreased and the market share of the domestic industry had increased following the introduction of the anti-dumping duties, the opposite would happen upon removal of the duties. We therefore find that the NTC did not provide a reasoned and adequate explanation of why these developments were likely to occur, and not just possible." The same distinction is material here. A sunset review necessarily involves a prediction concerning future circumstances, and the Commission is not required to demonstrate that injury already exists. It must, however, identify a sufficient factual foundation for concluding that injury is likely to recur. The majority of the Tribunal found that the Commission had not adequately discharged that obligation. Having regard to the contents of Table-VII and the reasoning accompanying the determination, that conclusion was reasonably open to the majority on the record before it.

109. The submissions advanced by Mr. Waqas Amir, particularly with reference to Table-VII, essentially invite this Court to adopt a different appreciation of the same evidence. Learned counsel maintains that the landed cost of Chinese imports, calculated without the anti-dumping duty, remained below the domestic industry's selling price and that the resulting margin of 2.3% was sufficient to establish the likelihood of renewed price undercutting. The learned Chairman of the Tribunal accepted that interpretation, whereas the majority considered the evidence insufficient to sustain the Commission's prediction. The difference C.M.A Nos. 28 & 29 of 2026 Page 63 of 64 between these conclusions concerns the probative value of the material and the inference reasonably to be drawn from it.

110. Whether a potential undercutting margin of 2.3%, viewed alongside the domestic industry's market share of 83.66% and its improved economic indicators, establishes the probability of future injury is principally a question involving the evaluation of evidence. The statutory responsibility for examining that evaluation was entrusted to the Tribunal under section 70(8). As already discussed, the appellate jurisdiction of this Court under section 70(13) does not extend to substituting its own assessment merely because another conclusion may also be reasonably possible. The appellants were required to demonstrate a material error of law, misreading or non-reading of the record, or a failure to apply the governing statutory standard. No such defect has been established. The majority examined the relevant material, identified deficiencies in the Commission's reasoning and furnished reasons for its conclusion. The fact that the learned Chairman reached a different conclusion upon the same evidence does not, without more, justify interference. Accordingly, the challenge to the majority's findings concerning the likelihood of injury also fails.

111. For the reasons recorded above, I am satisfied that the appellants have failed to establish any legal infirmity in the impugned judgment warranting interference in the exercise of appellate jurisdiction under section 70(13) of the Act. The Tribunal was competent to decide the appeal notwithstanding the expiry of the period prescribed under section 70(5), and the majority acted within the limits of its statutory powers in examining whether the Commission had properly established the relevant facts and evaluated them in an unbiased and objective manner. Its conclusions concerning the likelihood of recurrence of dumping and injury are supported by the deficiencies identified in the Commission's determination and do not disclose any material error of law. Consequently, C.M.A. No.28 of 2026 and C.M.A. No.29 of 2026 are dismissed, and the judgment dated 04.05.2026 passed by the Anti-Dumping Appellate Tribunal in Appeal No.519 of 2022 is maintained. There shall be no order as to costs. C.M.A Nos. 28 & 29 of 2026 Page 64 of 64 112. Before parting with the judgment, it is necessary to reiterate that the periods prescribed under sub-sections (5) and (6) of section 70 are intended to ensure the expeditious determination of disputes having significant commercial and fiscal consequences. Although non-compliance does not, by itself, invalidate the proceedings, the Tribunal remains under a statutory obligation to observe those requirements in letter and spirit. Where exceptional circumstances prevent disposal within the prescribed period, the reasons for such delay ought to be recorded, and every reasonable effort should be made to conclude the proceedings without further unnecessary adjournment. The Registrar shall transmit a copy of this judgment to the Chairman of the Tribunal for information and appropriate compliance with the statutory requirements governing the timely disposal of appeals.
